questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $2\text{A}\xrightarrow{k}\text{B}$ is a zero-order reaction, where $k=1.0$ mol L$^{-1}$ min$^{-1}$. If the initial concentration of A is $2$ M, then the time taken to complete $75\%$ of the reaction will be
questions.solution:
For a zero-order reaction $2\text{A} \rightarrow \text{B}$, the rate of reaction is expressed as:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = k$

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = 2k$

Integrating this equation, we get the integrated rate law:

$[\text{A}]_0 - [\text{A}]_t = 2kt$

Given:
Initial concentration, $[\text{A}]_0 = 2$ M
Rate constant, $k = 1.0$ mol L$^{-1}$ min$^{-1}$

For $75\%$ completion of the reaction, the amount of A reacted is:

$[\text{A}]_0 - [\text{A}]_t = \dfrac{75}{100} \times 2 = 1.5$ M

Substituting these values into the integrated rate equation:

$1.5 = 2 \times 1.0 \times t$

$2t = 1.5$

$t = 0.75$ min

Following data is for a reaction between reactants A and B :
The order of the reaction with respect to $A$ and $B$, respectively, are
questions.solution:
Let the rate equation is
Rate $=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}]^{\mathrm{x}}[\mathrm{B}]^{\mathrm{y}}$
Therefore, we can write
$2 \times 10^{-3}=k[0.1] \times\left[0.1 \rrbracket^y\right.$...(i)
$4 \times 10^{-3}=k[0.2]^x[0.1]^y$...(ii)
$1.6 \times 10^{-2}=\mathrm{k}[0.2]^{\times}[0.2]^{\mathrm{y}}$...(iii)
(ii) $\div$ (i);
$\frac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{-3}}=\frac{k[0.2]^x[0.1]^y}{k[0.1]^x[0.1]^y}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2}{1}=\frac{(0.2)^x}{(0.1)^x}=\left(\frac{2}{1}\right)^x$
$\therefore \quad x=1$
(ii) $\div$ (iii);
$\frac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{1.6 \times 10^{-2}}=\frac{k[0.2]^{\mathrm{x}}[0.1]^y}{\mathrm{k}[0.2]^{\mathrm{x}}[0.2]^{\mathrm{y}}}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{4}=\frac{(0.1)^y}{(0.2)^y}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^y$
$\therefore \quad y=2$
$\therefore \quad$ Rate $=k[A]^1[B]^2$
First order with respect to A while second order with respect to B .

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List I with List II :
List I (Order of reaction)List II (Unit of rate constant)
A. Zero orderI. $\text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{L}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
B. First orderII. $\text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{L}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
C. Second orderIII. $\text{s}^{-1}$
D. Third orderIV. $\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
The unit of rate constant $k$ for an $n$-th order reaction is given by $(\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-n}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

For zero order reaction ($n=0$):
Unit $= (\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-0}\ \text{s}^{-1} = \text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (Matches A with IV)

For first order reaction ($n=1$):
Unit $= (\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-1}\ \text{s}^{-1} = \text{s}^{-1}$ (Matches B with III)

For second order reaction ($n=2$):
Unit $= (\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-2}\ \text{s}^{-1} = \text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{L}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (Matches C with I)

For third order reaction ($n=3$):
Unit $= (\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-3}\ \text{s}^{-1} = \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{L}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (Matches D with II)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

Answer: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For an elementary chemical reaction, the Arrhenius plot is given below.

If the energy of activation is $6.64$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ and R $=8.3$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, the temperature at which the rate constant becomes $e^2$ min$^{-1}$, is
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation:

$\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$

For a plot of $\ln k$ versus $1/T$, the y-intercept corresponds to $\ln A$. From the given graph, the line intersects the y-axis at $6$.

Therefore, $\ln A = 6$.

We are given:
$E_a = 6.64 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 6640 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$R = 8.3 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$
$k = e^2 \text{ min}^{-1}$, which gives $\ln k = \ln(e^2) = 2$

Substituting these values into the Arrhenius equation:

$2 = 6 - \dfrac{6640}{8.3 \times T}$

$\dfrac{6640}{8.3 \times T} = 6 - 2$

$\dfrac{6640}{8.3 \times T} = 4$

$T = \dfrac{6640}{4 \times 8.3}$

$T = \dfrac{6640}{33.2}$

$T = 200 \text{ K}$

Answer: $200$ K

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below is an expression for the rate constant of a first order reaction occurring at a certain temperature, $T$ (K).
$\ln k = 14.34 - \dfrac{1.25 \times 10^{4}}{T}$
The energy of activation in kcal mol$^{-1}$ for the reaction is :
(Given : $k$ in s$^{-1}$, $R = 1.987$ cal mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The Arrhenius equation is given by:

$\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$

The given equation is:

$\ln k = 14.34 - \dfrac{1.25 \times 10^{4}}{T}$

Comparing the two equations:

$\dfrac{E_a}{R} = 1.25 \times 10^{4}$

$E_a = 1.25 \times 10^{4} \times R$

Substituting $R = 1.987$ cal mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$:

$E_a = 1.25 \times 10^{4} \times 1.987$

$E_a = 24837.5$ cal mol$^{-1}$

$E_a = 24.8375$ kcal mol$^{-1} \approx 24.84$ kcal mol$^{-1}$

Answer: $24.84$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Rate constants of a reaction at 500 K and $700 \mid \mathrm{K}$ are $0.04 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and $0.14 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, respectively; then, activation energy of the reaction is :
(Given: $\log 3.5=0.5441, \mathrm{R}=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{K}=A e^{-E_a / R T}$
After taking In both side
$\ln K=\ln A-\frac{E_a}{R T}$
$\operatorname{In} \mathrm{K}_1=\ln \mathrm{A}-\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{RT}_1}$ at temp. $\mathrm{T}_1$...(i)
$\operatorname{In} \mathrm{K}_2=\ln \mathrm{A}-\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{RT}_2}$ at temp. $\mathrm{T}_2$,,(ii)
(ii) - (i)
$\operatorname{In} K_2-\operatorname{InK} K_1=\frac{E_a}{R}\left[\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right]$
$\ln \frac{\mathrm{K}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{R}}\left[\frac{1}{500}-\frac{1}{700}\right]$
$\ln \frac{0.14}{0.04}=\frac{E_a}{R}\left[\frac{700-500}{500 \times 700}\right]$
$\ln \frac{14}{4}=\frac{E_a}{R}\left[\frac{200}{500 \times 700}\right]$
$\log 3.5=\frac{E_a}{2.303 \times R}\left[\frac{1}{250 \times 7}\right]$
$0.5441=\frac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.31}\left[\frac{1}{250 \times 7}\right]$
$E_a=0.5441 \times 8.31 \times 250 \times 7 \times 2.303$
$=0.5441 \times 83.1 \times 25 \times 7 \times 2.303$
$=18222.65$
$\approx 18219 \mathrm{~J}$

The rate of a reaction quadruples when temperature changes from $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $57^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Calculate the energy o activation.
Given $\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, \log 4=0.6021$

questions.q:
For a reaction $3 \mathrm{~A} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{~B}$
The average rate of appearance of $B$ is given by $\frac{\Delta[B]}{\Delta t}$. The correct relation between the average rate of appearance of $B$ with the average rate of disappearance of $A$ is given in option
questions.solution:
For reaction, $3 \mathrm{~A} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{~B}$
Average rate of reaction $=-\frac{1}{3} \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{A}]}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{B}]}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$
So $\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{B}]}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=-\frac{2}{3} \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{A}]}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one labelled as Assertion A and other is labelled as Reason R:

Assertion A: A reaction can have zero activation energy

Reason R: The minimum extra amount of energy absorbed by reactant molecules so that their energy becomes equal to threshold value, is called activation energy.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.solution: Activation energy is defined as the minimum amount of extra energy required by a reacting molecule to get converted into a product. If${E}_{a} = 0$ , then according to Arrhenius equation $k = {Ae}^{- {E}_{a} / RT} = {Ae}^{0} = A$ . This implies that every collision results into a chemical reaction which cannot be true. So, a reaction cannot have zero activation energy.

questions.q: The half life of a first order reaction is 2000 years. If the concentration after 8000 years is $0.02 \mathrm{M}$, then the initial concentration was :
questions.solution:
Half life period $\left(t_{1 / 2}\right)=2000$ years
$\begin{aligned}
k & =\frac{0.693}{2000} \\
k & =\frac{2.303}{t} \log \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_o}{[\mathrm{~A}]_t} \\
\frac{0.693}{2000} & =\frac{2.303}{8000} \log \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_o}{0.02} \\
\therefore \quad[\mathrm{A}]_o & =0.32 \mathrm{M}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a certain reaction $R \rightarrow$ Product, the plot of concentration $[R]$ vs time has a negative slope as shown. The order of reaction is :
questions.solution:
From the given graph, the plot of concentration $[R]$ versus time $t$ is a straight line with a negative slope.

The equation for this straight line can be written as:
$y = mx + c$
$[R] = (\text{slope}) \times t + \text{intercept}$

Given that the intercept is $[R_0]$ and the slope is $-k$, the equation becomes:
$[R] = -kt + [R_0]$

This equation represents the integrated rate law for a zero-order reaction. For a zero-order reaction, the rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of the reactant:
$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{d[R]}{dt} = k[R]^0 = k$

Integrating both sides:
$\int_{[R_0]}^{[R]} d[R] = -k \int_0^t dt$
$[R] - [R_0] = -kt$
$[R] = -kt + [R_0]$

Since the graph matches this equation, the order of the reaction is $0$.

Answer: $0$

questions.q:
Mechanism of a hypothetical reaction ${X}_{2} + {Y}_{2} \to 2XY$ is given below:

(i) ${X}_{2} \to X + X\left(fast\right)$

(ii) $X + {Y}_{2} ⇌ XY + Y\left(slow\right)$

(iii) $X + Y \to XY\left(fast\right)$

The overall order of the reaction will be
questions.solution:
The solution of this question is given by assuming step $( i )$ to be reversible which is not given in question

$Overallrate = Rateofsloweststep ( ii )$

$= k\left[X\right]\left[{Y}_{2}\right]$ ......$( i )$

K$=$rate constant of step $( ii )$

Assuming step $( i )$ to be reversible, its equilibrium constant,

${k}_{eq} = \dfrac{{\left[X\right]}^{2}}{\left[{X}_{2}\right]} ⇒ \left[X\right] = {k}_{eq}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\left[{X}_{2}\right]}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}$ .....$( ii )$

Put $( ii )$ in $( i )$

Rate $= k{k}_{eq}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\left[{X}_{2}\right]}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}\left[{Y}_{2}\right]$

Overall order $= \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 = \dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the activation energy for a reaction if its rate doubles when the temperature is raised from $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $35^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ?\left(R=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given, initial temperature,
$T_1=20+273=293 \mathrm{~K}$
Final temperature
$\begin{aligned}
T_2 & =35+273 \\
& =308 \mathrm{~K} \\
R & =8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$
Since, rate becomes double on raising temperature,
$\therefore r_2=2 r_1 \text{$ or $} \frac{r_2}{r_1}=2$
As rate constant, $k \propto r\therefore \frac{k_2}{k_1}=2$
From Arrnhenius equation, we know that
$\begin{aligned}
& \log \frac{k_2}{k_1}=-\frac{E_2}{2.303 R}\left[\frac{T_1-T_2}{T_1 T_2}\right] \\
& \log 2=-\frac{E_2}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left[\frac{293-308}{293 \times 308}\right] \\
& 0.3010=-\frac{E_2}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left[\frac{-15}{293 \times 308}\right]
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}
\therefore E_2 & =\frac{0.3010 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 293 \times 308}{15} \\
& =34673.48 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}=34.7 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: In a reaction, $A+B \rightarrow$ Product, rate is doubled when the concentration of $B$ is doubled, and rate increases by a factor of 8 when the concentrations of both the reactants $(A$ and $B$ ) are doubled. Rate law for the reaction can be written as
questions.solution:
Let the order of reaction with respect to A and B$ is $x and y$ respectively. So, the rate law can be given as
$R=k[A]^x[B]^y$
When the concentration of only $B$ is doubled, the rate is doubled, so
$R_1=k[A]^x[2 B]^y=2 R$
If concentrations of both the reactants A and B$ are doubled, the rate increases by a factor of 8 , so
$\begin{aligned}
R^{\prime \prime}=k[2 A]^x[2 B]^y & =8 R \\
\Rightarrow k 2^x 2^y[A]^x[B]^y & =8 R
\end{aligned}$
From Eq. (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& \Rightarrow & \frac{2 R}{R}$ & =$\frac{[A]^x[2 B]^y}{[A]^x[B]^y} \\
& \therefore & =2^y \\
& y & =1
\end{array}$
From Eq. (i) and (iv), we get
$\Rightarrow \frac{8 R}{R}=\frac{2^x 2^y[A]^x[B]^y}{[A]^x[B]^y} or 8=2^x 2^y
Substitution of the value of $y$ gives,
\begin{aligned}
& 8=2^x 2^1 \\
& 4=2^x
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}
& & (2)^2 & =(2)^x \\
\therefore & & x & =2
\end{aligned}$
Substitution$ of the value ofx and y$ in Eq. (i) gives,
$R=k[A]^2[B]$

questions.q: In a zero order reaction for every $10^{\circ}$ rise of temperature, the rate is doubled. If the temperature is increased from $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the rate of the reaction will become
questions.solution:
For $10^{\circ}$ rise in temperature, $n=1$ so rate $=2^n=2^1=2$
When temperature is increased from $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, change in temperature $=100-10=90^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, i.e., $n=9$
So, rate $=2^9=512$ times
Alternate method With every $10^{\circ}$ rise in temperature, rate becomes double, so $\frac{r^{\prime}}{r}=2^{\left(\frac{100-10}{10}\right)}=2^9=512$ times.

questions.q:
For a reaction, activation energy $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=0$ and the rate constant at $200 \mathrm{~K}$ is $1.6 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. The rate constant at $400 \mathrm{~K}$ will be
[Given that gas constant $\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
Key Idea Rate constants at two different temperatures is given by Arrhenius equation as follows:
$$
\log \frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303 R}\left[\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right], T_2>T_1
$$
Given, $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=0, \mathrm{~T}_1=200 \mathrm{~K}, \mathrm{k}_1=1.6 \times 10^6 $$\mathrm{~s}^{-1} 
\mathrm{T}_2=400 \mathrm{~K}, \mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$
According to Arrhenius equation,
$$
\log \frac{\mathrm{k}_2}{\mathrm{k}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \mathrm{R}}\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{~T}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{~T}_2}\right]
$$
On substituting the given values in above equation, we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log \frac{\mathrm{k}_2}{1.6 \times 10^6}=\frac{0}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left[\frac{\mathrm{l}}{200}-\frac{\mathrm{l}}{400}\right] \\
& \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{k}_2}{1.6 \times 10^6}\right)=0 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{k}_2}{1.6 \times 10^6}=10^0=1 \\
& \mathrm{k}_2=1.6 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \text{ at } 400 \mathrm{~K}
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus, option (2) is correct.$

(1) On doubling the initial concentration of $A$ only, the rate of reaction is also doubled and
(2) On doubling the initial concentrations of both $A$ and $B$, there is a change by a factor of 8 in the rate of the reaction.
The rate of this reaction is, given by
questions.solution:
For the reaction, $\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B} \longrightarrow$ Products
On doubling the initial concentration of A only, the rate of reaction is also doubled, therefore

$\text{ Rate } \propto[\mathrm{A}]^$1

Let initially rate law is

$\text{ Rate }=$k[A][B]^y

If concentration of and both are doubled, the rate gets changed by a factor of 8 .

$\begin{array}{r}8 \times \text{ Rate }$=$\mathrm{k}$[2 $\mathrm{~A}$][2 $\mathrm{~B}$]^${\mathrm{y}}$ \quad \ldots($\text{ iii) }$\\
{$\left[\because \text{ Rate } \propto[\mathrm{A}]^1$\right]$}

$\begin{aligned}$& 8=2 $\times$2^y \\

Hence, rate law is, rate $=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2$

questions.q: The rate constants $k_1$ and $k_2$ for two different reactions are $10^{16} \cdot e^{-2000 / T}$ and $10^{15} \cdot e^{-1000 / T}$, respectively. The temperature at which $k_1=k_2$ is
questions.solution:
Key Idea : The Arrhenius equation is represented as
$k=A e^{-E_a / R T}$
In the given equations, first take log and then compare them.
$\begin{aligned}
& k_1=10^{16} e^{-2000 / T} \\
& k_2=10^{15} e^{-1000 / T}
\end{aligned}$
On taking log, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& \log k_1=\log 10^{16}-\frac{2000}{2.303 T} \\
& \log k_2=\log 10^{15}-\frac{1000}{2.303 T} \\
& \because k_1=k_2
\end{aligned}$
Hence, from Eqs (i) and (ii)
$T=\frac{1000}{2.303} \mathrm{~K}$

questions.q:
The reaction of hydrogen and iodine monochloride is given as:
$\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{ICl}_{(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{HCl}_{(g)}+\mathrm{I}_{2(g)}$
This reaction is of first order with respect to $\mathrm{H}_{2(g)} and \mathrm{lCl}_{(g)+}$ following mechanisms were proposed
Mechanism A:
$\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{ICl}_{(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{HCl}_{(g)}+\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}$
Mechanism B:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{ICl}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCl}_{(g)}+\mathrm{HI}_{(g)} \text{ :slow } \\
& \mathrm{Hl}_{(g)}+\mathrm{lCl}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCl}_{(g)}+\mathrm{l}_{2(g)} \text{; fast }
\end{aligned}$
Which of the above mechanism(s) can be consistent with the given information about the reaction?
questions.solution:
The slowest step is the rate determining step thus the mechanism $\mathrm{B}$ will be more consistent because it involve one molecule of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and one molecule of ICl. It can be expressed as
$r=k\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right][\mathrm{ICl}]$
Related Theory
The rate determining step in a reaction mechanism is characterised by high activation energy. Usually, the first step is the slow step since it has the highest activation energy.

($\log 4=0$.60, $\log 5=0$.69)
questions.solution:
For a first order reaction
$k=\frac{2.303}{t} \log \frac{a}{a-x}$
When t=60 and $x=60 \% \begin{aligned}
k & =\frac{2.303}{60} \log \frac{100}{100-60} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{60} \log \frac{100}{40} \\
& =0.0153
\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned}
t^{1 / 2} & =\frac{2.303}{0.0153} \log \frac{100}{100-50} \\
& =\frac{2.303}{0.0153} \times \log 2 \\
& =\frac{2.303}{0.0153} \times 0.3010 \\
& =45.31 \mathrm{~min}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Consider the reaction: $\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow$ $2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}$
The equality relationship between $\frac{d\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]}{d t}$ and $-\frac{d\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]}{d t}$ is:
questions.solution:
For the reaction
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{N}_2(g)+3 \mathrm{H}_2(g) & \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(g) \\
\frac{-d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2\right]}{d t} & =-\frac{1}{3} \frac{d}{d t}\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right] \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \frac{d}{d t}\left(\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]\right) \\
\therefore \frac{d}{d t}\left(\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]\right) & =-\frac{2}{3} \frac{d}{d t}\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.q: For a first order reaction $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ the reaction rate at reactant concentration of $0.01 \mathrm{M}$ is found to be $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$ $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The half life period of the reaction is:
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned}$& $\text{ rate$ of reaction }=2 $\times$10^{-5} $\mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$\\ & \Rightarrow $\text{ order$ of reaction is }n=1 \\ & $\text{ rate }=\mathrm{K}[\mathrm{A}]^$n \\ & {[$\mathrm{~A}]$}=0.01 $\mathrm{M}$\\ & \Rightarrow \quad $\mathrm{K}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.01}=$2 $\times$10^{-3} \\ & $\mathrm{~K}=\frac{0.693}{t_{1 / 2}}$\\ & t_{1 / 2}=$\frac{0.693}{2 \times 10^{-3}}=$346.5 $\mathrm{~s} \end{aligned}$Related Theory For a first-order reaction, a graph plotted with $\ln [A]$ on the $Y$-axis and time on the $X$-axis, will be a straight line with a slope of $-k$.

questions.q: Reaction $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ follows first order kinetics. The time taken for 0.8 mole of $A$ to produce 0.6 mole of $B$ is 1 hour. What is the time taken for conversion of 0.9 mole of A to produce 0.675 mole of $\mathrm{B}$ ?
questions.solution:
For first order reaction,
\(\mathrm{k}=\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{t}} \log \frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{x}} \ldots \ldots .(1)\)
Where \(k\) is rate constant
when 0.8 mol of \(A\) produces 0.6 mol of \(B\) then, \(0.8-0.6=0.2\) moles of A is left .
final moles \(\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{x}=0.2\)
initial moles \(\mathrm{a}=0.8\)
\(\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{t}=\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{k}} \log \frac{0.8}{\mathrm{o} .2} \\
& \mathrm{k}=\frac{2.303}{1} \log [4] \ldots \ldots . . (2) \\
& \mathrm{k}=2.303 \times 0.6020 \\
& \mathrm{k}=1.3865 \ldots \ldots . .(3)
\end{aligned}\)
In second case, 0.9 moles of A produces 0.675 moles of \(B\) so remaining moles of \(A\) are \(0.9-0.675=0.225\)
final moles of \(\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{x}=0.225\)
initial mole \(=0.9\)
By using first order equation,
\(\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{t} & =\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{k}} \log \frac{0.9}{\mathrm{o} .225} \\
\mathrm{t} & =\frac{2.303}{1.3865} \log (4) \ldots . . (4) \\
\mathrm{t} & =1.661 \times 0.6020 \\
\mathrm{t} & =0.999=1 \mathrm{hr}
\end{aligned}\)

questions.solution:
The activation energy for the reverse reaction, $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}(\mathrm{rev})}$, is the difference between the product energy and transition state at the peak of the diagram. $\mathrm{H}_r$ is the difference between the potential energy of the reactant and the potential energy of the product.

In a reversible reaction of bi-molecular type the activation energy for forward reaction is positive. Whereas, for the backward reaction activation energy is negative.

In the reaction,

the time taken for $75 %$ reaction of $P$is twice the time taken for$50 %$ reaction of $P$. The concentration of $Q$varies with reaction time as shown in the figure.The overall order of the reaction is:
questions.solution:
The reaction is:

$\text{P} + \text{Q} \to \text{R} + \text{S}$
$rateofthereaction = k{\left[P\right]}^{x}{\left[Q\right]}^{y}$
The concentration of Q varies with time as per the graph by the equation.
$\left[\text{Q}\right] = \left[{\text{Q}_{0}\right] - \text{kt ​}$ i.e. Zero-order kinetics.

$⇒ y = 0$
With respect to reactant $P$

let time taken for $50 %$ completion of the reaction is $a$.

Then the time is taken for $75 %$  complication will be $2a .

$P\overset{{t}_{50 %}}{\to}$\dfrac{P}{2}$\overset{{t}_{75 %}}{\to}$\dfrac{P}{4}

at

$t = 0; [ P{]}_{0 %} = P$
$t = {t}_{50 %}; [ P{]}_{50 %} = $\dfrac{P}{2}
$t = {t}_{75 %}; [ P{]}_{75 %} = $\dfrac{P}{4}
As we can see,$ in each time interval of 'a' min the reactant concentration is changing by factor half. therefore rate constant is independent of the concentration of the reactantP$. hence with respect of reactant $P$, order of the reaction is $1$. 

$⇒ x = 1$
Rate law expression is $rate = k{$\left[P\right]$}^{1}{$\left[Q\right]$}^{0}$
The overall order of reaction $= x + y = 1 + 0 = 1$

$

$\dfrac{{N}_{0}}{N} - \dfrac{1}{e} = 5{N}_{0} ( t - 1 )$
$\dfrac{{N}_{0}}{N} = 5{N}_{0} ( t - 1 ) + \dfrac{1}{e}$
$\dfrac{{N}_{0}}{N} = 5{N}_{0}t + \left(\dfrac{1}{e} - 5{N}_{0}\right)$

questions.q:
Consider the following reversible first order reaction of $X$ at an initial concentration $\left[X\right]{}_{0} .$ The values of the rate constants are ${K}_{f} = 2{s}^{- 1} and {K}_{b} = 1{s}^{- 1}$
$X\mathop{⇌}_{{K}_{b}}^{{K}_{f}}Y$
A plot of concentration of $X and Y$ as function of time is
questions.solution:
For first order reaction,

$X ⇌ Y$

Given, ${K}_{f} = 2{s}^{- 1}$

${K}_{b} = 1{s}^{- 1}$

$∴ {K}_{eq} = \dfrac{{K}_{f}}{{K}_{b}} = \dfrac{\left[Y\right]}{\left[X\right]}$

${K}_{eq} = \dfrac{2}{1} = \dfrac{\left[Y\right]}{\left[X\right]}$

$⇒ 2\left[X\right] = \left[Y\right]$

or $2{\left[X\right]}_{eq} = {\left[Y\right]}_{eq}$

$∴ \left[Y\right] > \left[X\right]$

Thus, as the rate of reaction increases, there will be increased in the concentration ${Y}_{eq},$ but it will be less than initial concentration of $X\left({X}_{0}\right),$ whereas the concentration of ${X}_{eq}$ decreases.

\end{aligned}\)
(iii) concentration decreases$ with time.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The half-life of a first-order reaction is $20 \text{ min}$ at $300 \text{ K}$ and $2 \text{ min}$ at $350 \text{ K}$. The activation energy of the reaction is:
(Given: $2.303 \times R = 19.15 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$, $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ is inversely proportional to the half-life ($t_{1/2}$):
$k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}$

Therefore, the ratio of rate constants at the two temperatures is:
$\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{20 \text{ min}}{2 \text{ min}} = 10$

Using the Arrhenius equation:
$\log \dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2} \right]$

$\log(10) = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15} \left[ \dfrac{350 - 300}{300 \times 350} \right]$

$1 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15} \left[ \dfrac{50}{105000} \right]$

$1 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2100} \right]$

$E_a = 19.15 \times 2100 = 40215 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$

Converting to kilojoules per mole:
$E_a = 40.215 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $40.215 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The gas-phase decomposition of sulfuryl chloride is a first-order reaction:
$\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{SO}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$

The initial pressure of $\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ is $0.5 \text{ atm}$. After $100 \text{ s}$, the total pressure of the reaction mixture becomes $0.75 \text{ atm}$. The rate constant for the reaction is:
questions.solution:
For the first-order gas-phase reaction:
$\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{SO}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$

Let the initial pressure be $P_i$ and the decrease in pressure at time $t$ be $x$.
At $t = 0$: $P_i$, $0$, $0$
At $t = 100 \text{ s}$: $P_i - x$, $x$, $x$

Total pressure at time $t$, $P_t = (P_i - x) + x + x = P_i + x$
Therefore, $x = P_t - P_i$

The partial pressure of the reactant at time $t$ is:
$P_A = P_i - x = P_i - (P_t - P_i) = 2P_i - P_t$

Given $P_i = 0.5 \text{ atm}$ and $P_t = 0.75 \text{ atm}$:
$P_A = 2(0.5) - 0.75 = 1.0 - 0.75 = 0.25 \text{ atm}$

The first-order rate constant is:
$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log\dfrac{P_i}{P_A}$

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{100} \log\dfrac{0.5}{0.25} = \dfrac{2.303}{100} \log 2$

$k = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3010}{100} = \dfrac{0.693}{100} = 6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

Answer: $6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a certain chemical reaction, the plot of half-life ($t_{1/2}$) versus the initial concentration of the reactant ($[R_0]$) yields a horizontal straight line parallel to the concentration axis. The order of this reaction is:
questions.solution:
For a zero-order reaction, the half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[R_0]}{2k}$.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life is independent of the initial concentration: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$.

Since the plot of $t_{1/2}$ versus $[R_0]$ is a horizontal line parallel to the concentration axis, it indicates that $t_{1/2}$ is constant and does not change with $[R_0]$.

This independence from initial concentration is a characteristic feature of a first-order reaction.

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For a chemical reaction, the plot of $\ln[\text{R}]$ versus time $t$ yields a straight line with a slope of $-0.02 \text{ s}^{-1}$. How much time will it take for the concentration of the reactant to drop from $0.8 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ to $0.1 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$?
(Given : $\ln 2 = 0.693$, $\log 2 = 0.301$)
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate equation is:
$\ln[\text{R}] = -kt + \ln[\text{R}]_0$
The plot of $\ln[\text{R}]$ versus $t$ is a straight line with slope $= -k$.
Given slope $= -0.02 \text{ s}^{-1}$, we have $k = 0.02 \text{ s}^{-1}$.

The half-life of the reaction is:
$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.02} = 34.65 \text{ s}$

The concentration drops from $0.8 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ to $0.1 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$, which is a reduction to $\dfrac{1}{8}$ of the initial amount.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order reaction, what is the ratio of the time required for $99\%$ completion to the time required for $90\%$ completion?
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the time required is given by the integrated rate equation:

$t = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log\left(\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\right)$

For $99\%$ completion, the amount remaining is $[A]_t = 100 - 99 = 1\%$ of $[A]_0$.
$t_{99\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log\left(\dfrac{100}{1}\right) = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 2$

For $90\%$ completion, the amount remaining is $[A]_t = 100 - 90 = 10\%$ of $[A]_0$.
$t_{90\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log\left(\dfrac{100}{10}\right) = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log(10) = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 1$

Taking the ratio of the two times:
Ratio = $\dfrac{t_{99\%}}{t_{90\%}} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2$.

Answer: $2$

questions.solution:
The slope of a linear plot is determined by comparing its equation to the straight-line equation $y = mx + c$, where $m$ is the slope.

A. For a zero-order reaction, the integrated rate equation is $[R] = -kt + [R]_0$. A plot of $[R]$ versus $t$ gives a straight line with a slope of $-k$. (A matches IV)

C. For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate equation can be written as $\log[R] = -\dfrac{k}{2.303}t + \log[R]_0$. A plot of $\log[R]$ versus $t$ gives a straight line with a slope of $-\dfrac{k}{2.303}$. (C matches II)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For two different chemical reactions, the following graphical behaviors are observed:

Reaction A: A plot of the rate of reaction versus the concentration of the reactant is a straight line passing through the origin.
Reaction B: A plot of the half-life of the reaction versus the initial concentration of the reactant is a straight line passing through the origin.

The order of Reaction A and Reaction B, respectively, are:
questions.solution:
For Reaction A, the plot of rate versus concentration is a straight line passing through the origin. This implies that the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of the reactant (Rate $= k[R]$). This is the characteristic of a first-order reaction.

For Reaction B, the plot of half-life ($t_{1/2}$) versus initial concentration ($[R]_0$) is a straight line passing through the origin. This indicates that the half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration ($t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[R]_0}{2k}$). This is the characteristic of a zero-order reaction.

Therefore, Reaction A is first order and Reaction B is zero order.

Answer: First order, Zero order

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The half-life of a zero order reaction is $20 \text{ min}$ when the initial concentration of the reactant is $0.4 \text{ M}$. The time required for the concentration of the reactant to drop to $0.1 \text{ M}$ is:
questions.solution:
For a zero order reaction, the rate constant $k$ is calculated from the half-life as:

$k = \dfrac{[A]_0}{2t_{1/2}}$

$k = \dfrac{0.4 \text{ M}}{2 \times 20 \text{ min}} = 0.01 \text{ M min}^{-1}$

The integrated rate equation for a zero order reaction is:

$[A]_t = [A]_0 - kt$

Rearranging to solve for time $t$:

$t = \dfrac{[A]_0 - [A]_t}{k}$

$t = \dfrac{0.4 \text{ M} - 0.1 \text{ M}}{0.01 \text{ M min}^{-1}} = \dfrac{0.3}{0.01} = 30 \text{ min}$

Alternatively, since the concentration drops at a constant rate in zero order kinetics, a $0.2 \text{ M}$ drop takes $20 \text{ min}$ (one half-life), so a $0.3 \text{ M}$ drop takes $30 \text{ min}$.

Answer: $30 \text{ min}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The temperature dependence of the rate constant ($k$) for a chemical reaction is given by the empirical equation:
$\ln k = 10 - \dfrac{5000}{T}$
where $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin. Based on the Arrhenius equation, the pre-exponential factor ($A$) and the activation energy ($E_a$) for this reaction are respectively:
questions.solution:
The standard logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation is:
$\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$

The given empirical equation is:
$\ln k = 10 - \dfrac{5000}{T}$

Comparing the two equations term by term:
1) Intercept: $\ln A = 10 \Rightarrow A = e^{10}$
2) Slope term: $\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{5000}{T}$
$\dfrac{E_a}{R} = 5000 \Rightarrow E_a = 5000 R$

Thus, the pre-exponential factor is $e^{10}$ and the activation energy is $5000 R$.

Answer: $A = e^{10}$, $E_a = 5000 R$

Match List-I with List-II for a first-order reaction:

List-I (Percentage completion)List-II (Time required)
(A) $75\%$(I) $10 \times t_{1/2}$
(B) $87.5\%$(II) $3.32 \times t_{1/2}$
(C) $90\%$(III) $2 \times t_{1/2}$
(D) $99.9\%$(IV) $3 \times t_{1/2}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the time required for completion is given by $t = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \dfrac{100}{100-x}$.

For $75\%$ completion:
$t_{75\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \dfrac{100}{25} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log 4 = 2 \times \dfrac{2.303 \log 2}{k} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$.

For $87.5\%$ completion:
$t_{87.5\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \dfrac{100}{12.5} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log 8 = 3 \times \dfrac{2.303 \log 2}{k} = 3 \times t_{1/2}$.

For $90\%$ completion:
$t_{90\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \dfrac{100}{10} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log 10$.
Since $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3010}{k}$, we have $t_{90\%} = \dfrac{t_{1/2}}{0.3010} \approx 3.32 \times t_{1/2}$.

For $99.9\%$ completion:
$t_{99.9\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \dfrac{100}{0.1} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log 1000 = 3 \times \dfrac{2.303}{k} \approx 3 \times 3.32 \times t_{1/2} \approx 10 \times t_{1/2}$.

Thus, the correct matching is (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a reaction with zero activation energy, the plot of $\ln k$ versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is a straight line passing through the origin.

Reason (R): For a reaction with zero activation energy, the rate constant is independent of temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation, $k = A e^{-\dfrac{E_a}{RT}}$.

For a reaction with zero activation energy ($E_a = 0$), the equation becomes $k = A e^0 = A$. This shows that the rate constant $k$ is independent of temperature, making Reason (R) true.

Taking the natural logarithm, we get $\ln k = \ln A$. The plot of $\ln k$ versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$ will be a horizontal straight line with a slope of zero and a y-intercept of $\ln A$. It will not pass through the origin (unless $A=1$, which is not a general case). Therefore, Assertion (A) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a reaction between reactants X and Y, it is observed that doubling the concentration of X while keeping the concentration of Y constant increases the reaction rate by a factor of 8. Furthermore, halving the concentration of Y while keeping the concentration of X constant reduces the reaction rate to half of its initial value. The overall order of the reaction is
questions.solution:
Let the rate law be $\text{Rate} = k[\text{X}]^m[\text{Y}]^n$.

When the concentration of X is doubled, the rate increases by a factor of 8:
$2^m = 8 \Rightarrow m = 3$

When the concentration of Y is halved, the rate is halved:
$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow n = 1$

The overall order of the reaction is the sum of the partial orders:
$\text{Overall order} = m + n = 3 + 1 = 4$.

Answer: 4

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a given rise in temperature, a reaction with a higher activation energy shows a greater percentage increase in its rate constant compared to a reaction with a lower activation energy.

Reason (R): The rate constant of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to its activation energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
From the Arrhenius equation, the relationship between rate constants at two temperatures is:

$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right)$

For a constant temperature interval ($T_2 - T_1$), the value of $\log(k_2/k_1)$ is directly proportional to the activation energy ($E_a$). Therefore, a reaction with a higher $E_a$ will have a larger ratio of $k_2/k_1$, meaning it exhibits a greater percentage increase in its rate constant. Thus, the Assertion (A) is true.

According to the Arrhenius equation, $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$. This indicates that the rate constant decreases exponentially as the activation energy increases. It is not directly proportional to the activation energy. Thus, the Reason (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the rate constant is $2.303 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$. What percentage of the initial reactant will remain unreacted after $1000 \text{ s}$?
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate equation is:

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}$

Substituting the given values:

$2.303 \times 10^{-3} = \dfrac{2.303}{1000} \log \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}$

$1 = \log \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}$

$\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t} = 10^1 = 10$

$[A]_t = \dfrac{[A]_0}{10} = 0.1 [A]_0$

The percentage of reactant remaining is:

$\dfrac{[A]_t}{[A]_0} \times 100 = 0.1 \times 100 = 10\%$

Calculating $90\%$ is a common mistake where the percentage of decomposed reactant is found instead of the remaining reactant.

Answer: $10\%$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A first-order reaction has an activation energy of $22.98 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. If the rate constant of the reaction at $300 \text{ K}$ is $k$, at what temperature will the rate constant become $10k$?
(Given: $2.303 \times R = 19.15 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$\log \dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2} \right]$

Given:
$k_1 = k$
$k_2 = 10k$
$T_1 = 300 \text{ K}$
$E_a = 22.98 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 22980 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$2.303 \times R = 19.15 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:
$\log \left(\dfrac{10k}{k}\right) = \dfrac{22980}{19.15} \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - 300}{300 \times T_2} \right]$

$\log(10) = 1200 \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right]$

$1 = 1200 \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right]$

$300 T_2 = 1200 T_2 - 360000$

$900 T_2 = 360000$

$T_2 = 400 \text{ K}$

questions.question:
A first-order reaction has an activation energy of $22.98 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. If the rate constant of the reaction at $300 \text{ K}$ is $k$, at what temperature will the rate constant become $10k$?
(Given: $2.303 \times R = 19.15 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$\log \dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2} \right]$

Given:
$k_1 = k$
$k_2 = 10k$
$T_1 = 300 \text{ K}$
$E_a = 22.98 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 22980 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$2.303 \times R = 19.15 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:
$\log \left(\dfrac{10k}{k}\right) = \dfrac{22980}{19.15} \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - 300}{300 \times T_2} \right]$

$\log(10) = 1200 \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right]$

$1 = 1200 \left[ \dfrac{T_2 - 300}{300 T_2} \right]$

$300 T_2 = 1200 T_2 - 360000$

$900 T_2 = 360000$

$T_2 = 400 \text{ K}$

Answer: $400 \text{ K}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The temperature dependence of the rate constant ($\mathrm{k}$) for a chemical reaction is given by the equation:

$\ln \mathrm{k} = 15 - \dfrac{8000}{\mathrm{T}}$

where $\mathrm{T}$ is the temperature in Kelvin. What is the activation energy ($\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}$) for this reaction?
(Given $\mathrm{R} = 8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$\mathrm{k} = \mathrm{A} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}} / \mathrm{RT}}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides gives:
$\ln \mathrm{k} = \ln \mathrm{A} - \dfrac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{RT}}$

Comparing this with the given equation $\ln \mathrm{k} = 15 - \dfrac{8000}{\mathrm{T}}$, we get:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{R}} = 8000$

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}} = 8000 \times \mathrm{R}$
$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}} = 8000 \times 8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}} = 66512 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = 66.51 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

Mistakes in distractors:
Option 1 assumes the equation is in base-10 logarithm and incorrectly multiplies by 2.303.
Option 2 incorrectly assumes the coefficient of $1/\mathrm{T}$ is $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}$ directly in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, forgetting to multiply by $\mathrm{R}$.
Option 4 incorrectly divides the slope by $\mathrm{R}$ instead of multiplying.

Answer: $66.51 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a zero-order reaction $3\text{X} \rightarrow \text{Y}$, the initial concentration of X is $1.2$ M. If the half-life of the reaction is $20$ minutes, what is the value of the rate constant $k$?
questions.solution:
For the zero-order reaction $3\text{X} \rightarrow \text{Y}$, the rate of reaction is given by:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{X}]}{dt} = k$

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{d[\text{X}]}{dt} = 3k$

Integrating this equation yields the integrated rate law:

$[\text{X}]_0 - [\text{X}]_t = 3kt$

At the half-life ($t_{1/2} = 20$ min), the concentration of X drops to half of its initial value:

$[\text{X}]_t = \dfrac{1.2}{2} = 0.6$ M

Substituting the values into the integrated rate law:

$1.2 - 0.6 = 3 \times k \times 20$

$0.6 = 60k$

$k = \dfrac{0.6}{60} = 0.01$ M min$^{-1}$

Using the formula without accounting for the stoichiometric coefficient of $3$ leads to the incorrect answer of $0.03$ M min$^{-1}$.

Answer: $0.01$ M min$^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order gas-phase decomposition reaction, the half-life is $15$ minutes. If the initial partial pressure of the reactant is $800 \mathrm{~mm~Hg}$, what will be its partial pressure after $60$ minutes?
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the amount of reactant remaining after $n$ half-lives is given by $P_t = \dfrac{P_0}{2^n}$.

First, determine the number of half-lives ($n$) that have elapsed:
$n = \dfrac{\text{Total time}}{\text{Half-life}} = \dfrac{60 \text{ minutes}}{15 \text{ minutes}} = 4$

Now, calculate the partial pressure after $4$ half-lives:
$P_t = \dfrac{800 \mathrm{~mm~Hg}}{2^4}$
$P_t = \dfrac{800}{16} = 50 \mathrm{~mm~Hg}$

Dividing the initial pressure by $n$ ($800/4 = 200$) or by $2n$ ($800/8 = 100$) are common mistakes resulting from not using the exponential relationship.

Answer: $50 \mathrm{~mm~Hg}$

questions.q: For a zero order reaction, the rate constant is $1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1} \text{ s}^{-1}$. If the half-life of the reaction is $100 \text{ s}$, what is the initial concentration of the reactant?
questions.solution:
For a zero order reaction, the half-life is given by:

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[A]_0}{2k}$

Rearranging for initial concentration $[A]_0$:

$[A]_0 = 2 \times k \times t_{1/2}$

Substituting the given values:

$[A]_0 = 2 \times (1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1} \text{ s}^{-1}) \times 100 \text{ s}$

$[A]_0 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 100 = 0.30 \text{ M}$

Answer: $0.30 \text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the time required for $75\%$ completion is $40 \text{ minutes}$. The time required for $93.75\%$ completion of the same reaction will be:
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the amount of reactant remaining after $n$ half-lives is given by $\dfrac{N_0}{2^n}$.

At $75\%$ completion, the amount remaining is $100\% - 75\% = 25\%$.
Since $25\% = \dfrac{1}{4} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2$, this corresponds to $2$ half-lives.
Therefore, $2 \times t_{1/2} = 40 \text{ minutes} \Rightarrow t_{1/2} = 20 \text{ minutes}$.

At $93.75\%$ completion, the amount remaining is $100\% - 93.75\% = 6.25\%$.
Since $6.25\% = \dfrac{6.25}{100} = \dfrac{1}{16} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4$, this corresponds to $4$ half-lives.
The time required is $4 \times t_{1/2} = 4 \times 20 \text{ minutes} = 80 \text{ minutes}$.

Assuming a linear relationship (e.g., $50 \text{ minutes}$) or confusing $93.75\%$ with $87.5\%$ ($3$ half-lives, $60 \text{ minutes}$) leads to incorrect answers.

Answer: $80 \text{ minutes}$

questions.q: In a first-order reaction, the concentration of the reactant decreases from $1.0 \mathrm{M}$ to $0.25 \mathrm{M}$ in $40$ minutes. What will be the concentration of the reactant after a further $60$ minutes?
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the concentration drops from $1.0 \mathrm{M}$ to $0.25 \mathrm{M}$ (which is one-fourth of the initial concentration).

This corresponds to $2$ half-lives, since $\dfrac{1}{2^2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Thus, $2 \times t_{1/2} = 40 \text{ minutes}$, which gives $t_{1/2} = 20 \text{ minutes}$.

The question asks for the concentration after a further $60$ minutes. The total time elapsed from the start is $40 + 60 = 100 \text{ minutes}$.

Total number of half-lives, $n = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5$.

Final concentration $= \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2^n} = \dfrac{1.0}{2^5} = \dfrac{1.0}{32} = 0.03125 \mathrm{M}$.

Answer: $0.03125 \mathrm{M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a chemical reaction, the plot of $\ln k$ versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is a straight line with a negative slope.

Reason (R): The activation energy of a reaction decreases with an increase in temperature, leading to a higher rate constant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct. According to the Arrhenius equation, $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$. Taking the natural logarithm on both sides gives $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$. This represents a straight line equation ($y = mx + c$) where the slope is $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$, which is a negative value.

Reason (R) is not correct. The activation energy ($E_a$) of a reaction is characteristic of the reaction and is generally independent of temperature. The rate constant increases with temperature because a larger fraction of molecules acquires kinetic energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, not because the activation energy itself decreases.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

$k = \dfrac{4.606}{46.06}$

$k = 0.1\text{ min}^{-1}$

questions.q: The overall order of a chemical reaction is $1.5$. What will be the unit of the rate constant for this reaction?
questions.solution:
The unit of the rate constant $k$ for a reaction of $n$-th order is given by $(\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-n}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

Given that the overall order of the reaction is $n = 1.5$.

Substituting the value of $n$ in the general formula:
Unit of $k = (\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-1.5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
Unit of $k = (\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{-0.5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
Unit of $k = \text{mol}^{-0.5}\ \text{L}^{0.5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$

Therefore, the correct unit is $\text{mol}^{-0.5}\ \text{L}^{0.5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $\text{mol}^{-0.5}\ \text{L}^{0.5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a first-order reaction, the time required for $75\%$ completion is $1.5$ times the time required for $50\%$ completion.
Reason (R): The half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of the initial concentration of the reactant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, $50\%$ completion corresponds to exactly one half-life ($t_{1/2}$).

At $75\%$ completion, $25\%$ of the reactant remains, which is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the initial concentration. Reducing the concentration to one-fourth requires exactly two half-lives (from $100\%$ to $50\%$, then $50\%$ to $25\%$).

Thus, $t_{75\%} = 2 \times t_{50\%}$. Therefore, Assertion (A) is incorrect.

The half-life of a first-order reaction is given by $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$, which does not contain any concentration term and is thus independent of the initial concentration. Therefore, Reason (R) is correct.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A chemical reaction has an activation energy of $114.882 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. If the temperature is increased from $300 \mathrm{~K} to 600 \mathrm{~K}$, what is the ratio of the rate constant at the higher temperature to that at the lower temperature $\left(k_2/k_1\right)$?

(Given: $2.303 \times \mathrm{R} = 19.147 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \mathrm{R}} \left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$

Given:
$E_a = 114.882 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = 114882 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$T_1 = 300 \mathrm{~K}$
$T_2 = 600 \mathrm{~K}$
$2.303 \times \mathrm{R} = 19.147 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

Substitute the values into the equation:
$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \dfrac{114882}{19.147} \left(\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{600}\right)$

$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = 6000 \times \left(\dfrac{2 - 1}{600}\right)$

$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = 6000 \times \dfrac{1}{600} = 10$

Taking the antilogarithm (base 10) on both sides:
$\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 10^{10}$

Answer: $10^{10}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a zero-order reaction, the time required for 100% completion is exactly twice its half-life.
Reason (R): The rate of a zero-order reaction continuously decreases as the concentration of the reactant decreases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true. For a zero-order reaction, the time required for 100% completion is $t_{100\%} = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{k}$, while the half-life is $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2k}$. Thus, $t_{100\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$.

Reason (R) is false. By definition, a zero-order reaction has a constant rate that is independent of the concentration of the reactant. The rate does not decrease as the reactant is consumed.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of $100 \text{ s}$. If the initial concentration of the reactant is $0.2 \text{ M}$, what will be the instantaneous rate of the reaction after $200 \text{ s}$?
questions.solution:
The rate constant $k$ for a first-order reaction is related to its half-life by:

$k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{100} = 6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The time elapsed is $200 \text{ s}$, which corresponds to exactly two half-lives ($n = \dfrac{200}{100} = 2$).

The concentration of the reactant remaining after two half-lives is:

$[A]_t = \dfrac{[A]_0}{2^n} = \dfrac{0.2}{2^2} = \dfrac{0.2}{4} = 0.05 \text{ M}$

The instantaneous rate of the reaction at this time is given by the differential rate law:

$\text{Rate} = k[A]_t = (6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}) \times 0.05 \text{ M} = 3.465 \times 10^{-4} \text{ M s}^{-1}$

Using the initial concentration instead of the concentration at $200 \text{ s}$ leads to the incorrect initial rate of $1.386 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $3.465 \times 10^{-4} \text{ M s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a hypothetical chemical reaction, the activation energy is zero. If $k_1$ and $k_2$ are the rate constants of this reaction at temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively (where $T_2 > T_1$), which of the following relationships is correct?
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation, the relationship between rate constants at two different temperatures is given by:

$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$

Given that the activation energy ($E_a$) is zero, substituting $E_a = 0$ into the above equation yields:

$\log \left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = 0$

Taking the antilog on both sides gives:

$\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 1 \implies k_2 = k_1$

Thus, for a reaction with zero activation energy, the rate constant is independent of temperature.

Answer: $k_2 = k_1$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a chemical reaction, the temperature dependence of the rate constant $k$ is studied by plotting $\ln k$ versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$. If a positive catalyst is added to the reaction (assuming the pre-exponential factor remains constant), how will the resulting straight line change compared to the uncatalysed reaction?
options: The line will shift upwards parallel to the original line.
The slope of the line will become more negative.
The slope of the line will become less negative.
The intercept on the y-axis will decrease.
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation, $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$.

When $\ln k$ is plotted against $\dfrac{1}{T}$, a straight line is obtained with a slope equal to $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$ and a y-intercept equal to $\ln A$.

The addition of a positive catalyst provides an alternate pathway with a lower activation energy ($E_a$).

Since the new $E_a$ is smaller, the term $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$ becomes less negative (its magnitude decreases). Assuming the pre-exponential factor $A$ remains constant, the y-intercept is unchanged, but the slope becomes less negative, resulting in a flatter line.

Answer: The slope of the line will become less negative.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, a plot of half-life ($t_{1/2}$) on the y-axis versus the initial concentration ($[\text{A}]_0$) on the x-axis yields a straight line passing through the origin. If the slope of this line is $50 \text{ L mol}^{-1}\text{ s}$, the rate constant for the reaction is:
questions.solution:
For a zero-order reaction, the relationship between half-life and initial concentration is given by:

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2k}$

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line passing through the origin ($y = mx$), the slope ($m$) is:

$m = \dfrac{1}{2k}$

Given that the slope $m = 50 \text{ L mol}^{-1}\text{ s}$, we can solve for the rate constant $k$:

$k = \dfrac{1}{2m} = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 50} = \dfrac{1}{100} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The decomposition of nitrous oxide, $2\text{N}_2\text{O}(g) \rightarrow 2\text{N}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$, follows zero-order kinetics. If the initial concentration of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is $0.5$ M and the rate constant $k$ is $1.25 \times 10^{-3}$ M s$^{-1}$, what is the exact time taken for the reaction to reach $100\%$ completion?
questions.solution:
For the zero-order reaction $2\text{N}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2$, the rate of reaction is expressed as:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}]}{dt} = k$

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}]}{dt} = 2k$

The integrated rate law is:

$[\text{N}_2\text{O}]_0 - [\text{N}_2\text{O}]_t = 2kt$

For $100\%$ completion, the final concentration of the reactant is zero ($[\text{N}_2\text{O}]_t = 0$).

Substituting the given values ($[\text{N}_2\text{O}]_0 = 0.5$ M, $k = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}$ M s$^{-1}$):

$0.5 - 0 = 2 \times (1.25 \times 10^{-3}) \times t$

$0.5 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times t$

$t = \dfrac{0.5}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{500}{2.5} = 200$ s

Omitting the stoichiometric factor of $2$ in the rate equation leads to the incorrect time of $400$ s.

Answer: $200$ s

questions.q: The rate of a chemical reaction doubles when its temperature is increased from $300\text{ K}$ to $310\text{ K}$. Which of the following expressions correctly represents the activation energy ($E_a$) of the reaction in $\text{J mol}^{-1}$? (where $R$ is the universal gas constant)
questions.solution:
Given that the rate of reaction doubles, the ratio of rate constants $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 2$.
Initial temperature, $T_1 = 300\text{ K}$
Final temperature, $T_2 = 310\text{ K}$

Using the Arrhenius equation for two different temperatures:
$\log\left(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right)$

Substituting the given values:
$\log(2) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left(\dfrac{310 - 300}{300 \times 310}\right)$

$\log(2) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left(\dfrac{10}{300 \times 310}\right)$

Rearranging to solve for $E_a$:
$E_a = \dfrac{2.303 \times R \times 300 \times 310 \times \log 2}{10}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2.303 \times R \times 300 \times 310 \times \log 2}{10}$

questions.q: The half-life of a first-order reaction is $6.93\text{ minutes}$. The time required for the concentration of the reactant to drop from $0.4\text{ M}$ to $0.04\text{ M}$ is :
questions.solution:
First, calculate the rate constant ($k$) using the half-life formula for a first-order reaction:

$k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}$

Next, use the integrated rate law to find the time ($t$) required for the concentration to drop from $0.4\text{ M}$ to $0.04\text{ M}$:

$t = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}$

$t = \dfrac{2.303}{0.1} \log \dfrac{0.4}{0.04}$

$t = 23.03 \times \log(10)$

Since $\log(10) = 1$:

$t = 23.03\text{ min}$

Answer: $23.03\text{ min}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An elementary gas-phase reaction $2\text{A}(g) + \text{B}(g) \rightarrow \text{C}(g)$ is carried out in a closed vessel. If the volume of the reaction vessel is suddenly reduced to one-third of its original volume at constant temperature, the rate of the reaction will
questions.solution:
For an elementary reaction, the rate law is written directly from the stoichiometry of the balanced equation.

The rate law for the given reaction is:
$\text{Rate} = k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]$

When the volume of the closed vessel is reduced to $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of its original volume, the concentration (moles/volume) of each gaseous reactant increases by a factor of 3.

Let the new concentrations be $[\text{A}]' = 3[\text{A}]$ and $[\text{B}]' = 3[\text{B}]$.

The new rate of reaction is:
$\text{Rate}' = k(3[\text{A}])^2(3[\text{B}])$
$\text{Rate}' = k \times 9[\text{A}]^2 \times 3[\text{B}]$
$\text{Rate}' = 27 \times k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}] = 27 \times \text{Rate}$

Thus, the rate of the reaction increases by a factor of 27.

Answer: increase by a factor of 27.

questions.q:
For a zero-order reaction $2\text{A} \rightarrow 3\text{B}$ with rate constant $k$, consider the following statements:

(I) The rate of disappearance of A is $2k$.
(II) The half-life of the reaction is $\dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2k}$.
(III) The rate of appearance of B is $3k$.
(IV) The reaction goes to $100\%$ completion in time $t = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{k}$.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
For the zero-order reaction $2\text{A} \rightarrow 3\text{B}$, the rate of reaction is given by:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{B}]}{dt} = k$

Statement (I): The rate of disappearance of A is $-\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = 2k$. This statement is correct.

Statement (III): The rate of appearance of B is $\dfrac{d[\text{B}]}{dt} = 3k$. This statement is correct.

The integrated rate law for this reaction is:
$[\text{A}]_0 - [\text{A}]_t = 2kt$

Statement (II): At half-life ($t_{1/2}$), $[\text{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2}$.
$\dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2} = 2kt_{1/2} \Rightarrow t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{4k}$.
This statement is incorrect.

Statement (IV): For $100\%$ completion, $[\text{A}]_t = 0$.
$[\text{A}]_0 = 2kt \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2k}$.
This statement is incorrect.

Exactly two statements (I and III) are correct.

Answer: 2

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{B}]}{dt} = k$

Statement (I): The rate of disappearance of A is $-\dfrac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = 2k$. This statement is correct.

Statement (III): The rate of appearance of B is $\dfrac{d[\text{B}]}{dt} = 3k$. This statement is correct.

The integrated rate law for this reaction is:
$[\text{A}]_0 - [\text{A}]_t = 2kt$

Statement (II): At half-life ($t_{1/2}$), $[\text{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2}$.
$\dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2} = 2kt_{1/2} \Rightarrow t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{4k}$.
This statement is incorrect.

Statement (IV): For $100\%$ completion, $[\text{A}]_t = 0$.
$[\text{A}]_0 = 2kt \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{[\text{A}]_0}{2k}$.
This statement is incorrect.

Exactly two statements (I and III) are correct.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a reaction $A + B \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the rate constant has the unit $\text{L}^{2}\ \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. If the reaction is first order with respect to reactant $A$, what is the order of the reaction with respect to reactant $B$?
questions.solution:
The general unit for the rate constant $k$ of an $n$-th order reaction is $(\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{1-n}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

The given unit is $\text{L}^{2}\ \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$, which can be rewritten as $(\text{mol}\ \text{L}^{-1})^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

Equating the exponents:
$1 - n = -2$
$n = 3$

The overall order of the reaction is $3$.

The overall order is the sum of the partial orders with respect to each reactant:
Overall order = Order with respect to $A$ + Order with respect to $B$
$3 = 1 + \text{Order with respect to } B$
$\text{Order with respect to } B = 2$

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a first-order reaction, the time taken for $99\%$ completion is exactly twice the time taken for $90\%$ completion.

Reason (R): The time required for the completion of a given fraction of a first-order reaction is independent of its initial concentration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the time required for a specific percentage of completion is given by $t = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log\left(\dfrac{a_0}{a_0 - x}\right)$.

For $90\%$ completion:
$t_{90\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log\left(\dfrac{100}{100 - 90}\right) = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log(10) = \dfrac{2.303}{k}$

For $99\%$ completion:
$t_{99\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log\left(\dfrac{100}{100 - 99}\right) = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log(100) = 2 \times \dfrac{2.303}{k}$

Therefore, $t_{99\%} = 2 \times t_{90\%}$. Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) states that the time for fractional completion is independent of initial concentration, which is a true characteristic of first-order kinetics. However, this fact does not explain why $t_{99\%} = 2 \times t_{90\%}$. The factor of 2 arises from the properties of logarithms ($\log 10^2 = 2 \log 10$), not merely from the independence of initial concentration. Thus, both statements are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a first-order reaction, the plot of $\ln[R]$ versus time is a straight line with a y-intercept equal to $\ln[R]_0$.

Reason (R): The integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction is $\ln[R] = -kt + \ln[R]_0$, where $[R]_0$ is the initial concentration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
The integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction is $\ln[R] = -kt + \ln[R]_0$.

This equation is of the form $y = mx + c$, which represents a straight line. Here, $y = \ln[R]$, $x = t$, slope $m = -k$, and the y-intercept $c = \ln[R]_0$.

Thus, the plot of $\ln[R]$ versus time is a straight line that intersects the y-axis at $\ln[R]_0$.

Therefore, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) provides the mathematical basis that correctly explains Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the plot of $\log[R]$ against time ($t$ in seconds) yields a straight line with a slope of $-3.01 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$. The half-life of the reaction is:
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate equation is:

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log\dfrac{[R]_0}{[R]}$

Rearranging this equation gives:

$\log[R] = -\dfrac{k}{2.303}t + \log[R]_0$

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, the slope ($m$) of the plot of $\log[R]$ versus $t$ is $-\dfrac{k}{2.303}$.

Given slope $= -3.01 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

$-\dfrac{k}{2.303} = -3.01 \times 10^{-3}$

$k = 2.303 \times 3.01 \times 10^{-3} = 6.93 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

The half-life ($t_{1/2}$) for a first-order reaction is:

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{6.93 \times 10^{-3}} = 100 \text{ s}$

Answer: $100 \text{ s}$

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Slope of $\ln k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$(I) $\log_{10} A$
(B) Intercept of $\ln k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$(II) $-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R}$
(C) Slope of $\log_{10} k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$(III) $\ln A$
(D) Intercept of $\log_{10} k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$(IV) $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The Arrhenius equation is $k = A e^{-\dfrac{E_a}{RT}}$.

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides yields:
$\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$
Comparing this with the equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, a plot of $\ln k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$ has a slope of $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$ and an intercept of $\ln A$.

Converting the equation to base 10 logarithm gives:
$2.303 \log_{10} k = 2.303 \log_{10} A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$
$\log_{10} k = \log_{10} A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 RT}$
Comparing this with $y = mx + c$, a plot of $\log_{10} k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$ has a slope of $-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R}$ and an intercept of $\log_{10} A$.

Therefore, the correct matches are:
(A) Slope of $\ln k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T} \rightarrow -\dfrac{E_a}{R}$ (IV)
(B) Intercept of $\ln k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T} \rightarrow \ln A$ (III)
(C) Slope of $\log_{10} k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T} \rightarrow -\dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R}$ (II)
(D) Intercept of $\log_{10} k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T} \rightarrow \log_{10} A$ (I)

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The decomposition of ammonia on a platinum surface is a zero-order reaction:

$2\text{NH}_3(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g})$

If the initial concentration of $\text{NH}_3$ is $0.5$ M and the rate of appearance of $\text{H}_2$ is $6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ M min$^{-1}$, what will be the concentration of $\text{NH}_3$ remaining after $40$ minutes?
questions.solution:
For the zero-order reaction $2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2$, the rate of reaction is:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = k$

Given the rate of appearance of $\text{H}_2$ is $6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ M min$^{-1}$:
$\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt} = 3k = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ M min$^{-1}$
$\Rightarrow k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ M min$^{-1}$

The rate of disappearance of $\text{NH}_3$ is:
$-\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt} = 2k = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ M min$^{-1}$

Using the integrated rate law for the disappearance of $\text{NH}_3$:
$[\text{NH}_3]_0 - [\text{NH}_3]_t = 2kt$

Substitute the given values ($[\text{NH}_3]_0 = 0.5$ M, $t = 40$ min):
$0.5 - [\text{NH}_3]_t = (4.0 \times 10^{-3}) \times 40$
$0.5 - [\text{NH}_3]_t = 0.16$

$[\text{NH}_3]_t = 0.5 - 0.16 = 0.34$ M

The concentration of $\text{NH}_3$ remaining is $0.34$ M.

Answer: $0.34$ M

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Consider the decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface at high pressure. Which of the following graphical plots correctly represents the kinetics of this reaction?
options: A plot of reaction rate versus $[NH_3]$ is a horizontal line parallel to the concentration axis.
A plot of reaction rate versus $[NH_3]$ is a straight line passing through the origin.
A plot of half-life ($t_{1/2}$) versus initial concentration ($[NH_3]_0$) is a horizontal line parallel to the concentration axis.
A plot of $\ln[NH_3]$ versus time is a straight line with a negative slope.
questions.solution:
The decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface at high pressure is a classic example of a zero-order reaction.

For a zero-order reaction, the rate law is given by:
$\text{Rate} = k[NH_3]^0 = k$

This means the rate of the reaction is constant and independent of the concentration of the reactant. Therefore, a plot of reaction rate versus $[NH_3]$ will be a horizontal line parallel to the concentration axis.

The other options describe characteristics of a first-order reaction (where rate is directly proportional to concentration, half-life is independent of initial concentration, and $\ln[NH_3]$ versus time has a negative slope).

Answer: A plot of reaction rate versus $[NH_3]$ is a horizontal line parallel to the concentration axis.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The kinetic data for a chemical reaction is given in the following table:

Time (min)$0$$10$$20$
Concentration ($\mathrm{M}$)$0.40$$0.20$$0.10$


Based on the above data, what will be the concentration of the reactant at $40$ minutes?
questions.solution:
From the table, the concentration of the reactant reduces to half its initial value every $10$ minutes ($0.40 \mathrm{M} \rightarrow 0.20 \mathrm{M} \rightarrow 0.10 \mathrm{M}$).

This constant half-life indicates a first-order reaction with $t_{1/2} = 10 \text{ min}$.

We need to find the concentration at $t = 40 \text{ min}$.

Number of half-lives, $n = \dfrac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{40}{10} = 4$

Concentration after $4$ half-lives $= \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2^n} = \dfrac{0.40}{2^4} = \dfrac{0.40}{16} = 0.025 \mathrm{M}$.

Answer: $0.025 \mathrm{M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For a reaction $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the following initial rate data were obtained:

Experiment[A] (mol L$^{-1}$)[B] (mol L$^{-1}$)Initial Rate
10.10.1$R$
20.20.1$2R$
30.10.2$4R$


What will be the initial rate of the reaction when $[\text{A}] = 0.2$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{B}] = 0.2$ mol L$^{-1}$?
questions.solution:
Let the rate law be $\text{Rate} = k[\text{A}]^x[\text{B}]^y$.

From Experiment 1 and 2, keeping $[\text{B}]$ constant, doubling $[\text{A}]$ (from $0.1$ to $0.2$) doubles the rate (from $R$ to $2R$).
Therefore, the reaction is first order with respect to A ($x = 1$).

From Experiment 1 and 3, keeping $[\text{A}]$ constant, doubling $[\text{B}]$ (from $0.1$ to $0.2$) quadruples the rate (from $R$ to $4R$).
Therefore, the reaction is second order with respect to B ($y = 2$).

The rate law is $\text{Rate} = k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^2$.

When $[\text{A}] = 0.2$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{B}] = 0.2$ mol L$^{-1}$, both concentrations are doubled compared to Experiment 1.
New Rate $= k(2[\text{A}])(2[\text{B}])^2 = 2 \times 4 \times k[\text{A}][\text{B}]^2 = 8R$.

Answer: $8R$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the plot of $\log_{10} k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is a straight line with a slope of $-1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ K}$. What is the activation energy of the reaction? (Given $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$k = A e^{-\dfrac{E_a}{RT}}$

Taking logarithm to the base 10 on both sides:
$\log_{10} k = \log_{10} A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R T}$

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, the plot of $\log_{10} k$ vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$ gives a straight line with:
Slope ($m$) = $-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R}$

Given slope = $-1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ K}$
$-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} = -1.0 \times 10^4$

$E_a = 1.0 \times 10^4 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$E_a = 191471.4 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$E_a \approx 191.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Using $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$ instead of $-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303 R}$ leads to the incorrect answer of $83.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $191.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two different first-order reactions, X and Y, have rate constants $0.0693 \text{ min}^{-1}$ and $0.0231 \text{ min}^{-1}$ respectively. If both reactions start with the same initial concentration, what will be the ratio of the remaining concentrations of the reactants, $\dfrac{[\text{X}]}{[\text{Y}]}$, after $30 \text{ minutes}$?
questions.solution:
For reaction X:
$t_{1/2, \text{X}} = \dfrac{0.693}{k_{\text{X}}} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0693} = 10 \text{ min}$

Number of half-lives in $30 \text{ min}$ for X, $n_{\text{X}} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$

Remaining concentration of X, $[\text{X}] = \dfrac{[\text{X}]_0}{2^3} = \dfrac{[\text{X}]_0}{8}$

For reaction Y:
$t_{1/2, \text{Y}} = \dfrac{0.693}{k_{\text{Y}}} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0231} = 30 \text{ min}$

Number of half-lives in $30 \text{ min}$ for Y, $n_{\text{Y}} = \dfrac{30}{30} = 1$

Remaining concentration of Y, $[\text{Y}] = \dfrac{[\text{Y}]_0}{2^1} = \dfrac{[\text{Y}]_0}{2}$

Since the initial concentrations are equal ($[\text{X}]_0 = [\text{Y}]_0$), the ratio of their remaining concentrations is:
$\dfrac{[\text{X}]}{[\text{Y}]} = \dfrac{[\text{X}]_0 / 8}{[\text{Y}]_0 / 2} = \dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Therefore, the ratio is $1:4$.

Answer: $1:4$

When the concentration of P is halved and Q is quadrupled, the new rate becomes:
$\text{Rate}_{2} = k\left(\dfrac{[\text{P}]}{2}\right)\left(4[\text{Q}]\right)^{1/2}$

$\text{Rate}_{2} = k\left(\dfrac{[\text{P}]}{2}\right) \times 2[\text{Q}]^{1/2}$

$\text{Rate}_{2} = k[\text{P}][\text{Q}]^{1/2} = \text{Rate}_{1}$

Thus, the initial rate remains unchanged.

Answer: remain unchanged.

questions.q:
For a certain chemical reaction, the plot of $\ln k$ versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is a straight line with a slope of $-1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ K}$. What is the activation energy of the reaction?
(Given $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$k = A e^{-E_a / RT}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides yields:
$\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$

This represents the equation of a straight line ($y = mx + c$), where $y = \ln k$ and $x = \dfrac{1}{T}$.
The slope ($m$) of this line is $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$.

Equating the given slope to the theoretical expression:
$-\dfrac{E_a}{R} = -1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ K}$
$E_a = 1.0 \times 10^4 \times 8.314 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$E_a = 83140 \text{ J mol}^{-1} = 83.14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Using the factor $2.303$ is a common mistake that occurs when confusing the $\ln k$ plot with a $\log k$ plot.

Answer: $83.14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A first-order reaction takes $30$ minutes for $50\%$ completion. The time required for $93.75\%$ completion of the same reaction will be :
questions.solution:
The time required for $50\%$ completion is the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) of the reaction.
Therefore, $t_{1/2} = 30 \text{ minutes}$.

For $93.75\%$ completion, the percentage of reactant remaining is:
$100\% - 93.75\% = 6.25\%$

Convert the remaining percentage to a fraction:
$\dfrac{6.25}{100} = \dfrac{1}{16}$

Express the fraction in terms of powers of $1/2$:
$\dfrac{1}{16} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4$

This means $4$ half-lives are required for the reaction to be $93.75\%$ complete.
Total time = $n \times t_{1/2} = 4 \times 30 \text{ minutes} = 120 \text{ minutes}$.

Answer: $120 \text{ minutes}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a first-order chemical reaction, the rate constant $k$ follows the Arrhenius equation. Which of the following correctly describes the plot of the natural logarithm of its half-life ($\ln t_{1/2}$) versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$?
options: A straight line with a positive slope
A straight line with a negative slope
An exponential curve with a positive slope
A straight line passing through the origin
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, the half-life is given by:
$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$

According to the Arrhenius equation, $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$. Substituting this into the half-life expression gives:
$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{A e^{-E_a/RT}} = \left(\dfrac{0.693}{A}\right) e^{E_a/RT}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides, we get:
$\ln t_{1/2} = \ln\left(\dfrac{0.693}{A}\right) + \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$

This is in the form of a straight line equation, $y = mx + c$, where $y = \ln t_{1/2}$ and $x = \dfrac{1}{T}$.
The slope $m = \dfrac{E_a}{R}$, which is a positive value.
The intercept $c = \ln\left(\dfrac{0.693}{A}\right)$, which means the line does not pass through the origin.

Therefore, the plot is a straight line with a positive slope.

Answer: A straight line with a positive slope
